passages.happening:
Samuel comes to Saul with a word from the LORD. The LORD has seen what the Amalekites did to Israel when they ambushed them on the way up from Egypt (verses 1-2). “Now go and attack the Amalekites and devote to destruction all that belongs to them. Do not spare them, but put to death men and women, children and infants, oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys” (verse 3).

Saul gathers his army at Telaim (verse 4). Before he attacks, he warns the Kenites who live among the Amalekites to leave, ‘Since you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt’ (verse 6), and they go.

Saul strikes the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur, east of Egypt (verse 7). ‘He captured Agag king of Amalek alive’ (verse 8). Saul and his troops spare Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle and everything good. ‘They were unwilling to destroy them, but they devoted to destruction all that was despised and worthless’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This is the turning point of Saul's story. In chapter 13 Samuel said that Saul's line would not last. Here the LORD rejects Saul himself as king.

The chapter reaches back to Israel's beginnings. The Amalekites had attacked Israel in the wilderness soon after it left Egypt, and Deuteronomy adds that they struck the weary stragglers at the rear and ‘had no fear of God’. Israel was told to remember, and to blot out Amalek's memory once it had rest in the land. Saul is given that old, unfinished task.

The Amalekites were a desert people of the Negev and Sinai, the dry lands south of Judah, known in the Old Testament mainly as raiders. They appear as Israel's enemies from the wilderness through the judges and into David's day, when an Amalekite band burns Ziklag (chapter 30). So this campaign did not end them. Havilah and Shur mark a broad desert region toward Egypt; just where is uncertain.

To devote to destruction translates one Hebrew verb for the ban, herem. People or goods were given over wholly to God, so they could not be kept for human use. In war it meant total destruction, with no plunder taken. Israel did not invent it. The Moabite king Mesha, in an inscription from the ninth century BC, boasts of devoting an Israelite town to his god Chemosh. Under the ban, keeping the best animals was not a smaller obedience. It was taking from God what had been given to him.

The army numbers in verse 4 are large for the time, and some scholars think the word for thousand can also mean a military unit. Others take them as they stand.

Notice the Kenites. They lived among the Amalekites, and they were warned and spared because of the kindness they had shown Israel.
passages.later:
The command goes back to the LORD's word after Amalek's first attack: ‘I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven’ (Exodus 17:14), and to the charge in Deuteronomy: ‘Remember what the Amalekites did to you along your way from Egypt’ (Deuteronomy 25:17).

The Kenites were the clan of Moses' father-in-law, who had gone up with Judah into the land (Judges 1:16).
passages.hard:
How can God command the destruction of a whole people, children and infants included?

This is one of the hardest places in the Bible. The verse says ‘children and infants’, and nothing in these notes softens that. A reader who is grieved by it is reading with a conscience the Bible formed: “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers” (Deuteronomy 24:16).

Christians who receive this book as God's word read the command in several ways, as the site's pages on the conquest set out. Each has a cost.

Some read it as judgment on a people with a long record of attacking the weak, after long patience. The cost is the children, for whom this reading has no answer that takes the grief away.

Some read the language of total destruction as the stock idiom of ancient war, since Amalekites are alive and raiding a few chapters later (27:8; 30:1). The cost is that this eases the scale and not the substance. The text still presents the command as total, and it still says infants.

Some ground it in God's unique right over life, as Augustine and Thomas Aquinas did. The cost is that it does not show how anyone could know such a command was God's.

Some read these texts as God stooping to the understanding of an ancient people, to be seen in the light of Christ's command to love enemies. The cost is that the reader must decide which portraits of God to trust, and critics say this weakens the authority of Scripture.

Many hold more than one together. The site takes no side, and none of them makes the chapter easy.

Under all of them these things hold. The command was tied to one people at one moment, and it was never renewed. It was not about race: the Kenites who lived among the Amalekites were spared. The New Testament gives the church no war to wage. Jesus told his followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44), and said that ‘all who draw the sword will die by the sword’ (Matthew 26:52). And the chapter itself does not celebrate the killing. Its question is whether God's king will obey God, and it ends in grief.

So it must be said plainly. No people living today is Amalek. No one may use this chapter to justify violence or contempt toward any person or people, and it has no nation, state, land or conflict of today in view. Christians did later quote such chapters over their own wars. That was a misuse of the text, and the church must own it as sin.

Nothing here permits contempt for the Amalekites or for anyone. God says, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?” (Ezekiel 18:23).

The site's pages on the violence of the Old Testament and on the command to destroy the Canaanites go further.
passages.asks: Saul kept what he wanted and destroyed what was worthless, and called it obedience. Ask where you obey God in the parts that cost you nothing. And if this chapter troubles you, ask your questions honestly, as Abraham did when he asked whether the Judge of all the earth would do what is right.

passages.happening:
The word of the LORD comes to Samuel: “I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions” (verse 11). Samuel is distressed and cries out to the LORD all night.

In the morning he hears that Saul has gone to Carmel and set up a monument for himself, and then gone down to Gilgal (verse 12). When Samuel arrives, Saul greets him: ‘I have carried out the LORD’s instructions’ (verse 13).

“Then what is this bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle that I hear?” (verse 14). Saul says the troops spared the best animals to sacrifice to the LORD, and destroyed the rest (verse 15).

Samuel reminds him that he was once small in his own eyes, and that the LORD made him king and sent him on this mission. ‘So why did you not obey the LORD? Why did you rush upon the plunder and do evil in the sight of the LORD?’ (verse 19). “But I did obey the LORD,” Saul replied (verse 20). He brought back Agag, he says, and the troops took the best of the plunder to sacrifice at Gilgal (verses 20-21).

Samuel answers in poetry. “Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obedience to His voice? Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and arrogance is like the wickedness of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king” (verses 22-23).
passages.hearers:
Samuel's first response to God's word is not anger at Saul. He is distressed, and he cries out to the LORD all night.

The Carmel of verse 12 is a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Hebron, not the famous Mount Carmel on the northern coast. Saul's monument was a victory marker, the kind kings set up to honor themselves. The man who was once small in his own eyes is now building monuments to himself.

The verb to hear or obey runs through the chapter. Saul is told to listen (verse 1), he does not obey (verse 19), and soon he will admit that he feared the people and obeyed their voice (verse 24). He says he obeyed, and the animals are bleating behind him.

He also shifts the blame. The troops spared the animals, he says, and spared them for a sacrifice. Samuel's answer breaks into poetry and states the lesson of the chapter in matched lines. God wants a listening heart more than the fat of rams. Stubborn self-will is as serious in his eyes as the practices Israel despised, divination and household idols.

The verdict rests on a matched pair. Saul rejected the word of the LORD, so the LORD rejected him as king. The same verb described Israel's rejection of the LORD as king in chapter 8. Rejection answers rejection.
passages.later:
The prophets carried Samuel's saying on. “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6). “He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8).

A psalm puts it as a prayer: “For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it; You take no pleasure in burnt offerings. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:16-17).
passages.asks: Saul called his disobedience a sacrifice. Ask what religious activity you might be offering God in place of the obedience he actually asked for. And ask whose voice you obey when you are afraid of what people will think.

passages.t: A torn robe, and a final parting
passages.happening:
“I have sinned,” Saul says. He has broken the LORD's command ‘because I feared the people and obeyed their voice’ (verse 24). He asks Samuel to forgive him and come back with him to worship (verse 25). Samuel refuses: the LORD has rejected him as king (verse 26).

As Samuel turns to go, Saul grabs the hem of his robe, and it tears (verse 27). “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor who is better than you” (verse 28). “Moreover, the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind” (verse 29).

“I have sinned,” Saul replied. “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel” (verse 30). Samuel goes back with him, and Saul worships the LORD (verse 31).

Then Samuel has Agag brought to him. Agag comes thinking that the danger of death is past (verse 32). Samuel says, “As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women” (verse 33), and puts him to death before the LORD at Gilgal.

Samuel goes home to Ramah, and Saul to Gibeah. ‘And to the day of his death, Samuel never again visited Saul. Samuel mourned for Saul, and the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel’ (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Saul says ‘I have sinned’ twice. But his confession blames the people, asks at once to be honored before the elders, and centers on his own position. The chapter sets regret over consequences beside repentance that turns toward God, and Saul shows the first.

A garment could stand for a person's standing and authority, and tearing it could act out a verdict. Grabbing the hem of a robe was also a way of pleading. Saul's grip tears the prophet's robe, and Samuel turns the torn cloth into a sign: the kingdom has been torn from Saul and given to a better man, still unnamed.

Agag's death is told in one sentence and the story moves on. It is presented as the carrying out of the sentence Saul left undone. It is no model for anyone's treatment of a prisoner.

The chapter is framed by the LORD's regret (verses 11 and 35), with Samuel's statement that God does not change his mind set in the middle. The narrator leaves the tension for the reader to hold. And it ends in grief. Samuel never sees Saul again, and he mourns for him.
passages.later:
Centuries later a prophet tore his own cloak to show another king that God was tearing a kingdom away: “Take ten pieces for yourself, for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says” (1 Kings 11:31).

Balaam had said what Samuel says: ‘God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind’ (Numbers 23:19).

Later Jewish tradition connected Agag with Haman, the man who tried to destroy the Jews in Persia, called ‘Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite’ (Esther 3:1).
passages.hard:
The LORD ‘regretted’ making Saul king, yet Samuel says that God does not change his mind. How can both be true?

Theologians read the two statements in different ways, but most agree on this much. The first describes God's real grief and his response to human sin. The second denies that God changes his purposes the way people do. Taken together, they show a God who truly responds to what people do, and whose character and purposes are not fickle as a man's are. The chapter puts them side by side on purpose, and it does not resolve them for the reader.

The rejection in this chapter is of Saul as king. The chapter does not say what became of Saul before God, and these notes say nothing about any person's eternal state.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Saul's confession asked to be honored before the elders. Ask what your own confessions are really about, God or your reputation. And ask what it means that Samuel, who spoke the verdict, went on grieving for the man it fell on.
